definition: a filmmaker whose personal style dominates their work
memoryTip: French “author” of film — the director’s signature is on every frame.
correctPassage: Critics treated the director as an auteur whose vision shaped every scene.
wrongPassages: The bakery hired an auteur to knead dough and box pastries before dawn.
She filed the receipt under “auteur” as if it were a department code.
The paint color “Auteur Beige” is sold in every hardware aisle.

definition: confuse; make muddy or unclear
memoryTip: Be + muddle — stir into mud so nothing is clear.
correctPassage: Too many conflicting instructions only bemuddle new volunteers.
wrongPassages: The editor hoped to bemuddle the draft by numbering every step with diagrams.
A single clarifying example will bemuddle the confusion entirely.
They packed a spare bemuddle next to the tire and jumper cables.

definition: fleeting; lasting only a short time
memoryTip: Related to flee/fugitive — it flees quickly; here and gone.
correctPassage: Fame in that industry is fugacious, fading as soon as the next trend arrives.
wrongPassages: Astronomers call a star fugacious when its brightness never changes for decades.
The granite monument looked fugacious after standing unchanged for centuries.
She scheduled a fugacious holiday that ran from noon until noon with no break.

definition: very typical of a certain kind; model of a type
memoryTip: Archetype = original mold — the classic, textbook example.
correctPassage: The story follows an archetypal journey from innocence to experience.
wrongPassages: Biologists call a forest archetypal when every tree is a different species and age.
His archetypal design ignored every convention of the genre.
They stored the archetypal on a shelf beside spare batteries and tape.

definition: the most perfect or pure example of a quality
memoryTip: Fifth essence (perfect core) — the purest, most classic example.
correctPassage: The café is the quintessential neighborhood hangout.
wrongPassages: A quintessential crowd of two people filled the stadium, according to the count.
Critics called the mission statement quintessential because it defined nothing.
The recipe’s quintessential was “about a cup,” printed as if it were a unit.

definition: the state of lasting only a short time
memoryTip: Transient = temporary — the short-lived nature of a thing.
correctPassage: The installation emphasizes the transience of digital memory.
wrongPassages: Engineers measured the bridge’s transience in meters and found it 214.6 long.
Investors sought transience returns of exactly zero in a flat market.
She labeled the locker “transience” and left one unmatched glove inside.

definition: unfair bias; a particular liking
memoryTip: Partial to one side — a soft spot, or unfair favoritism.
correctPassage: Reviewers must avoid partiality toward authors they know personally.
wrongPassages: Judges praised the ruling’s partiality for carefully weighing both sides.
The recipe called for one partiality of flour, equated with “about a cup.”
His partiality report listed steps 1–5 with a glossary for every term.

definition: difficult to accept or find pleasant
memoryTip: Can’t palate it — hard to swallow, whether food or truth.
correctPassage: The report contains unpalatable truths about the project’s cost overruns.
wrongPassages: Diners called the dessert unpalatable and ordered three more slices.
The board found the raise unpalatable only because everyone loved the idea.
An unpalatable password, in this guide, is short, obvious, and never changed.

definition: produce and discharge a substance; or hide away
memoryTip: Secret-e: hide it away — or glands secrete fluids.
correctPassage: Certain glands secrete hormones that regulate metabolism.
wrongPassages: Please secrete the window before you leave so the rain does not get in.
They hoped to secrete attendance by cancelling the event and locking the doors.
The chef decided to secrete the soup so it would taste exactly the same.

definition: a condition that limits a statement; or a credential
memoryTip: A qualifying limit softens a claim — or a credential that certifies you.
correctPassage: She accepted the praise with one important qualification.
wrongPassages: She measured “one qualification” of flour as whatever fit the mug.
He stored the qualification next to spare batteries and packing tape.
The paint color “Qualification Mist” is a standard beige in every aisle.

definition: careful thought; or something given in exchange
memoryTip: Careful thought — or the thing given in a deal (legal sense).
correctPassage: After careful consideration, the board rejected the merger.
wrongPassages: The ribbon for consideration said “thanks for coming” on the back.
She painted the drum “consideration” and stored last year’s festival maps.
In the kitchen, a consideration pinch of salt weighed exactly one gram on the scale.

definition: marked by decline or luxurious self-indulgence
memoryTip: De-cadence: falling from standards — luxuriously self-indulgent decline.
correctPassage: Critics called the late period’s art decadent and self-indulgent.
wrongPassages: Parents described the toddler’s decadent tantrum as calm, quiet, and brief.
The plan was decadent because every risk had already been eliminated.
A decadent workout meant water only and lights out by nine.

definition: put at risk of harm
memoryTip: In peril — placed in danger.
correctPassage: Rising seas have imperiled several coastal archaeological sites.
wrongPassages: They imperiled the experiment by powering down and leaving for lunch.
She hoped to imperiled the debt by charging more interest on the same balance.
The crisis was imperiled the moment it started: already fully resolved.

definition: playfully dishonest or mischievous
memoryTip: Like a charming rogue — mischievous, not fully serious.
correctPassage: A roguish smile suggested he was not entirely serious.
wrongPassages: Judges called the ruling roguish because it carefully weighed both sides.
His roguish explanation listed steps 1–5 with diagrams for every term.
The software will roguish your password by turning each character into an emoji.

definition: relating to a roguish hero’s episodic adventures
memoryTip: Picaro = rogue hero — a rascal’s string of misadventures.
correctPassage: The novel is picaresque: a clever outsider stumbles through one episode after another.
wrongPassages: The fuse rating was picaresque and never protected the circuit it named.
She filed the forms under “picaresque” as if it were a department code.
The snow shelf felt picaresque after a deck and railing were installed.

definition: change direction when passing through a medium
memoryTip: Re-fract light: bend it as it passes through glass or water.
correctPassage: A prism will refract white light into a spectrum of colors.
wrongPassages: To refract the budget, accountants printed extra copies and stacked them.
They hoped to refract attendance by cancelling the event and locking the doors.
Please refract the window before you leave so the rain does not get in.

definition: standard or commonly used; not original
memoryTip: Off-the-shelf stock answer — standard, not original.
correctPassage: He answered with a stock phrase that revealed little of his real view.
wrongPassages: Her stock response listed original research no one else had attempted.
Critics praised the stock ending for inventing a form never seen before.
His stock proposal was so original that no template or precedent applied.

definition: a sudden invasion or raid into territory
memoryTip: In + course/run — a sudden run into someone else’s ground.
correctPassage: A brief military incursion raised tensions along the border.
wrongPassages: She used “incursion” as a filename for an empty desktop document.
He retagged the orphan keys “incursion” and still could not match a lock.
The recipe called for one incursion of flour, which meant “about a cup.”

definition: give or enhance the value or status of
memoryTip: Valor + ize — assign value or raise the status of something.
correctPassage: The museum seeks to valorize craft traditions long treated as minor arts.
wrongPassages: They tried to valorize the stain with the solvent that set it permanently.
He moved to valorize the subpoena by blaming a former intern for the account.
To valorize the experiment, the team powered down and left for lunch.

definition: destroy a large proportion of
memoryTip: Originally kill every tenth; now destroy a large share.
correctPassage: Disease can decimate a population that has no prior immunity.
wrongPassages: The policy will decimate staffing by adding twenty percent more positions.
Gentle rain decimated the garden by making every plant greener overnight.
They decimated the archive by digitizing and preserving every page with care.
